sections.title: Multivariate Data
rules: In multivariate data, each observation is a vector of d distinct features.
A dataset of N observations forms an N by d data matrix.
Each row of the data matrix represents a single observed instance.
Each column of the data matrix represents a single variable or feature.
Multivariate features can combine continuous, discrete, and binary variables.

sections.title: Parameter Estimation
rules: The sample mean vector contains the sample mean of each feature column.
The sample mean vector is an unbiased estimator of the population mean vector.
Covariance measures the linear association between two distinct variables.
The sample covariance matrix is a symmetric d by d matrix.
Diagonal elements of the covariance matrix represent individual feature variances.
Off-diagonal elements represent pairwise covariances between different features.
The correlation matrix normalizes covariances between negative one and positive one.

sections.title: Estimation of Missing Values
rules: Missing values occur when sensors fail or subjects skip questions.
Discarding instances with missing values discards useful information from observed features.
Mean imputation replaces each missing entry with the sample mean of that feature.
Regression imputation predicts the missing feature from the observed features.
The Expectation-Maximization algorithm estimates parameters iteratively in the presence of missing values.

sections.title: Multivariate Normal Distribution
rules: The multivariate normal distribution is defined by a mean vector and a covariance matrix.
The Mahalanobis distance measures distance between a point and the mean vector.
Mahalanobis distance scales distances by the inverse of the covariance matrix.
Contours of constant probability density form hyperellipsoids centered at the mean vector.
Eigenvectors of the covariance matrix determine the principal axes of the hyperellipsoids.
Eigenvalues of the covariance matrix determine the variances along the principal axes.
When the covariance matrix is spherical, Mahalanobis distance reduces to Euclidean distance.

sections.title: Multivariate Classification
rules: Multivariate classification models each class with a multivariate normal density.
Quadratic discriminant analysis allows each class to have an arbitrary covariance matrix.
Quadratic discriminant analysis produces quadratic, curved decision boundaries between classes.
Linear discriminant analysis assumes all classes share an identical covariance matrix.
Shared covariance cancels quadratic terms, producing linear hyperplane decision boundaries.
When covariance matrices are diagonal, features are conditionally independent given the class.
When covariance matrices are spherical, the classifier assigns instances to the nearest class mean.

sections.title: Tuning Complexity
rules: An unconstrained d by d covariance matrix requires estimating d times d plus one divided by two parameters.
When the number of features is large, full covariance matrices cause overfitting.
We reduce complexity by constraining covariance matrices to be shared, diagonal, or spherical.
Regularized discriminant analysis interpolates between class covariance, pooled covariance, and spherical identity matrices.
Cross-validation selects the regularization parameters that achieve the lowest classification error.

sections.title: Discrete Features
rules: Discrete features take values from a finite set of categories.
Binary features take values of zero or one.
The naive Bayes classifier assumes discrete features are conditionally independent given the class.
Under naive Bayes, the class-conditional probability is the product of individual feature probabilities.
Independent Bernoulli distributions model binary features.
Multinomial distributions model discrete features with more than two categories.

sections.title: Multivariate Regression
rules: Multivariate linear regression predicts a continuous target from a vector of input features.
The model computes the output as a linear combination of input features plus an intercept.
We find the optimal weight vector by solving the normal equations in matrix form.
The closed-form solution requires computing the inverse of the feature correlation matrix.
When predicting multiple response variables, we solve multivariate regression for each output dimension.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Harold Hotelling and P. C. Mahalanobis developed foundational theory for multivariate statistics.
Ronald Fisher introduced linear discriminant analysis for multivariate classification in nineteen thirty-six.
High dimensionality requires careful regularization to avoid the curse of dimensionality.
